statement: In people with amphetamine withdrawal or dependence (the review counts amphetamine, dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine) who were starting treatment, mostly young men in Thai treatment centres or a probation facility and one Australian outpatient group, the evidence is insufficient to say whether any medicine eases withdrawal: in a Cochrane review searched to May 2008 (four small randomized trials, 125 participants), neither of the two medicines tested, amineptine and mirtazapine, reduced withdrawal symptoms compared with placebo (standardized mean difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.38; two trials, 74 people), and amineptine did not reduce craving (one trial, 29 people). Amineptine reduced dropping out of treatment (RR 0.21, 0.07 to 0.69; two trials from one research group, 74 people) and improved clinician-rated overall condition (mean difference -0.49, -0.80 to -0.17), but it was withdrawn from the market in 1999 over misuse. Mirtazapine did not reduce dropping out (RR 0.98, 0.49 to 1.97; two trials, 51 people) or improve overall condition in the one trial with usable data, while a second small trial reported fewer withdrawal symptoms in figures that could not be combined. Side effects were not reported for any trial. The intervals are wide enough that a moderate benefit on symptoms cannot be ruled out. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Only two medicines have been tested in proper trials for the crash and withdrawal after stopping amphetamines, in four small trials of 125 people starting treatment. Neither made withdrawal symptoms or craving better than a dummy pill. One of them helped people stay in treatment, but it is no longer sold. The other did not help in the better-run trial, while a smaller trial reported some benefit. The trials were too small to rule out a modest benefit, and none of them reported on side effects.
population: People with DSM-IV amphetamine withdrawal (two trials of inpatients in a Thai drug-dependence treatment centre) or dependence (one trial in a Thai probation facility, one in Australian outpatient clinics); 110 men and 15 women; mean ages 18.5 to 31 in the four trials
exposure: Amineptine or mirtazapine, randomized and double-blind, during early abstinence (study conditions in the study card)
outcome: Withdrawal-symptom scores, craving, dropping out of treatment and clinician-rated global state at the end of treatment
magnitude: Withdrawal symptoms: SMD -0.08 (95% CI -0.54 to 0.38), two trials, 74 participants (amineptine -0.26, -0.86 to 0.34; mirtazapine 0.17, -0.54 to 0.89). Craving (amineptine; higher is less craving): MD 0.43 (-1.23 to 2.09), one trial, 29. Dropping out: amineptine RR 0.21 (0.07 to 0.69), two trials, 74; mirtazapine RR 0.98 (0.49 to 1.97), two trials, 51; both medicines together RR 0.52 (0.29 to 0.94), I2 45%. Global state (higher is worse): amineptine MD -0.49 (-0.80 to -0.17), two trials, 72; mirtazapine MD 0.30 (-0.22 to 0.82), one trial, 31. Numbers of people dropping out per group are shown only in forest plots (images); no number needed to treat is reported.

statement: In healthy young and middle-aged adults (not sleep-deprived, without psychiatric illness, and in the trial read in full never having used stimulants) tested in double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies, a single dose of a prescription stimulant taken by mouth, amphetamine (including Adderall, a mixture of amphetamine salts) or methylphenidate, compared with a placebo (dummy pill), is associated with at most small improvements on laboratory tests of thinking. In a meta-analysis of studies published or obtained to the end of 2012 (48 articles, 1,409 participants; Ilieva et al., 2015), the clearest effect was on inhibitory control, the ability to hold back an automatic response: about a fifth of a standard deviation (Hedges' g 0.20, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.30; 24 studies), unchanged after a trim-and-fill correction for possibly missing studies. Working memory improved by 0.13 (−0.02 to 0.27; 20 studies) and episodic memory tested soon after learning by 0.20 (0.01 to 0.38; 12 studies); after the correction, which used published studies only and d without Hedges' small-sample adjustment (so each fall is approximate), both shrank to estimates whose intervals include no effect (d 0.06, −0.08 to 0.20; d 0.12, −0.06 to 0.29), and two added studies with no effect would have been enough to make the short-term memory effect non-significant. Memory tested 1 hour to 1 week after learning improved by 0.45 (0.27 to 0.63; 11 studies), a medium effect that fell to d 0.26 (0.04 to 0.47) after correction and came mostly from one laboratory, whose seven studies, all in men, gave a lower dose (10 mg of amphetamine; study conditions), tended to use longer delays and supplied the six largest effects, so that dose, sex and laboratory cannot be told apart. Amphetamine and methylphenidate were not shown to differ. The review describes no protocol or registration, included only reports in English, did not assess the risk of bias of the studies it pooled, reports no funding, and includes the authors' own trial and unpublished data from their laboratory. In that trial (Ilieva et al., 2013; funded by the US Office of Naval Research), 46 healthy young adults (aged 21 to 30; 22 men, 24 women) who had never used stimulants each took a 20 mg capsule of mixed amphetamine salts before each of two test sessions (study conditions) and, a week apart in counterbalanced order, an identical placebo before two others: their scores improved on none of 13 measures of memory, working memory, inhibitory control, creativity, matrix reasoning (Raven's items) and SAT-type questions (the smallest p for a drug effect was .12; overall p = .17), in a sample sized to detect a medium effect (d = 0.5) on any one measure, so smaller effects could not be excluded. Participants nevertheless rated the active capsule as slightly more helpful (55.18 against 50.25 on a 1-to-100 line on which 50 meant no effect; p = .05), and how much more helpful each person found it was not significantly correlated with how much their scores changed (composite r = −.06); nobody was asked which capsule they thought they had taken, so the rating may reflect noticing a drug rather than a mistaken belief about performance. Gains in people of lower baseline ability on three measures came from uncorrected tests in subgroups of about 16 to 20 people (editors' reading of the degrees of freedom), and the interaction for one of them (Raven's matrices) was not significant (p = .10). Repeated or daily use, studying or exams, sleep loss and people who already use stimulants were not studied. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Across dozens of small laboratory studies, healthy adults who took a single dose of a prescription stimulant, amphetamine (as in Adderall) or methylphenidate, did a little better on some thinking tests than on a dummy pill: the clearest gain, in holding back an automatic response, was about a fifth of a standard deviation, and the memory gains shrank once possibly unpublished studies were allowed for. A bigger gain for memory tested hours to days later came mostly from one laboratory's studies in men. In the largest single trial read, 46 healthy young adults who had never used stimulants did no better on any of 13 tests on days they took an Adderall-type pill than on dummy-pill days, yet rated the pill as slightly more helpful than the dummy pill; how helped they felt was not clearly linked to how their scores changed, and nobody checked whether they could tell the pills apart. Daily use, studying, exams and sleep loss were not tested.
population: Healthy young and middle-aged adults without psychiatric illness and not sleep-deprived, in double-blind placebo-controlled laboratory studies published or obtained to the end of December 2012 (48 articles: 44 published reports, three unpublished data sets and one dissertation; 1,409 participants as reported; mostly within-person designs; children, older adults and criminal samples excluded); and, in the trial read in full, 46 Caucasian native English speakers aged 21 to 30 (22 men, 24 women) who had never used psychostimulants, recruited by advertisement around Drexel University and the University of Pennsylvania
exposure: A single dose of amphetamine (the authors' own trial of mixed amphetamine salts, the Adderall formulation, is coded as amphetamine) or methylphenidate, taken by mouth before testing (study conditions: the review coded 20 mg or more of amphetamine and 40 mg or more of methylphenidate as high doses, with testing 30 minutes to 4.5 hours after the dose; the trial gave a 20 mg capsule of mixed amphetamine salts before each of two test sessions, with testing after 75 minutes)
comparator: Placebo, double-blind, mostly in the same people on another occasion (within-person crossover); in the trial, a visually identical placebo capsule a week apart from the drug sessions, with order counterbalanced
outcome: Scores on laboratory tests of inhibitory control, working memory, and episodic memory tested soon after learning or 1 hour to 1 week later (review); 13 measures of memory, working memory, inhibitory control, convergent creativity, Raven's matrices items and SAT-type questions, and a 1-to-100 rating of how the pill had affected that day's performance (trial)
magnitude: Ilieva et al. (2015), random-effects Hedges' g against placebo, scaled by the placebo-condition SD (primary) and by the SD of within-person change (secondary); trim-and-fill values are d from published studies only, without Hedges' correction, so each fall is approximate: inhibitory control 0.20 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.30), 24 studies, Q(23) = 7.82, I² = 0; change-score 0.19 (0.11 to 0.26); trim-and-fill unchanged; fail-safe N 39. Working memory 0.13 (−0.02 to 0.27), 20 studies; change-score 0.13 (0.06 to 0.20), 23 studies; trim-and-fill 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.20) and 0.06 (−0.03 to 0.15). Short-term episodic memory 0.20 (0.01 to 0.38), 12 studies; change-score 0.22 (0.09 to 0.35); trim-and-fill 0.12 (−0.06 to 0.29); fail-safe N 2. Delayed episodic memory 0.45 (0.27 to 0.63), 11 studies; change-score 0.44 (0.26 to 0.62); lower dose 0.64 (0.40 to 0.88) against higher dose 0.20 (−0.08 to 0.48), Q(1) = 5.49, p = .02, confounded with laboratory, male-only samples and longer delays; trim-and-fill 0.26 (0.04 to 0.47); fail-safe N 59. Ilieva et al. (2013), n = 46 (36 to 46 per measure): MANOVA across 13 measures F(13, 13) = 1.71, p = .17; no drug main effect significant (smallest p = .12, Remote Associations, F(1, 42) = 2.56); perceived enhancement 55.18 (SD 14.87) against 50.25 (SD 3.95), F(1, 40) = 4.09, p = .05; correlation of perceived with actual enhancement on a composite r = −.06, p = .76 (10 of 11 single measures not significant; Go/No-go r = .33, p = .04). Editors' arithmetic: the fail-safe N values of 39, 2 and 59 are all below the review's own threshold for calling them large (5k + 10, with k the number of published studies analysed: 120 for inhibitory control, 65 for short-term and for delayed memory).

evidence.extracted: Systematic search of PubMed and PsycInfo (amphetamine or methylphenidate combined with task and construct terms), the reference lists of four reviews and the list of articles under review by an American Academy of Neurology committee on cognitive enhancement on which the last author serves, for research published to the end of December 2012; researchers active in the area were asked for unpublished data and 14 requests were made for missing data, yielding two data sets of studies in progress or in submission, extra data from four published reports and an unpublished pilot data set from the authors' laboratory. Any report format was eligible, but only reports in English; participants had to be young or middle-aged adults (children, older adults, and criminal or mentally ill samples excluded, as were studies with sleep deprivation); a double-blind, placebo-controlled design was required, a criterion the authors say aimed to maximize methodological quality; interventions were amphetamine or methylphenidate taken by mouth once before testing (the only study of repeated dosing was excluded), with testing 30 minutes to 4.5 hours after amphetamine and 40 minutes to 4.5 hours after methylphenidate. Of 1,799 records (1,505 after removing duplicates), 1,304 were excluded on title and 201 assessed; exclusions included 73 for an out-of-scope cognitive construct, eighteen without a double-blind placebo-controlled design, seven not in English and 19 without data to compute an effect size (not imputed); 48 articles were analysed (44 published reports, three unpublished data sets and one dissertation, with 1,409 participants). Eligibility was decided independently by the first two authors; the first author coded all studies and the second independently coded a random 44% of means and standard deviations (intraclass correlation above .99). High doses were coded as amphetamine 20 mg or more and methylphenidate 40 mg or more (study conditions). No risk-of-bias tool, protocol or registration is described.

evidence.extracted: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Participants: 46 Caucasian native English speakers, 22 men and 24 women, aged 21 to 30 (mean 24, SD 2.88), who answered advertisements around Drexel University and the University of Pennsylvania inviting them to tests of memory, creativity, intelligence and personality; excluded were people who reported a history of neurological or psychiatric disease or other conditions that rule out stimulants, people taking other stimulants or interacting drugs, people whose caffeine consumption was estimated to exceed 700 mg a day, and anyone who had previously used psychostimulants (to rule out sensitization and tolerance). Each took a capsule of 20 mg mixed amphetamine salts (the formulation sold as Adderall, dextro- and levo-amphetamine 3:1; study conditions; the drug supplied by the University of Pennsylvania's Investigational Drug Service) before each of the two sessions of the drug condition (one SAT session and one cognitive-battery session, at least two days apart) and a visually indistinguishable placebo capsule before the other two. Two drug-free baseline sessions always came first; in the four on-pill sessions the order of drug and placebo was counterbalanced (24 and 22 participants), with the drug and placebo pairs a week apart; participants were randomly assigned, double-blind, to take the drug or the placebo capsule (no further detail of the allocation is given), and testing began after a 75-minute wait; urine drug tests were done at each on-pill session. risk_of_bias.note: The review applied no risk-of-bias tool and handled quality only by requiring double-blind placebo-controlled designs, so the randomization or counterbalancing of order, allocation concealment and selective reporting of the pooled studies cannot be appraised (card sc_ilieva_2015, AMSTAR 2: critically low confidence, first pass). The trial read in full is at some concerns (card sc_ilieva_2013, RoB 2): sequence generation not described, 10 of 46 without usable data on one measure, no blinding check, which matters most for the perceived-enhancement rating, and no correction for multiple comparisons.

inconsistency.note: No measurable heterogeneity in any pool (I² = 0; with 11 to 24 mostly small studies this is weak evidence of homogeneity). The larger delayed-memory effect comes with a stated explanation, a confounded cluster of one laboratory's low-dose, male-only studies with longer delays, which the statement reports; the trial's null result fits small pooled effects, which it was not sized to detect.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for single doses, laboratory tests and healthy, rested adults, and says that repeated use, studying or exams, sleep loss and people who already use stimulants were not studied; the trial's participants had never used stimulants.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: the pooled intervals are narrow enough to show that the average single-dose effects are small (upper limits 0.27 to 0.38 for three constructs; 0.63 for delayed memory before correction); the trial alone could not detect effects below about half a standard deviation, which the statement says.

publication_bias.note: Funnel-plot asymmetry and trim-and-fill reduced three of the four pooled estimates (working memory to 0.06 and short-term memory to 0.12, both with intervals including zero, and delayed memory from 0.45 to 0.26; trim-and-fill values are d from published studies only, so each fall is approximate), and the fail-safe N values (39, 2, 59) are all below the review's own threshold for robustness (editors' arithmetic: 120 for inhibitory control, 65 for each memory pool); 19 eligible studies lacked usable data and seven non-English reports were excluded. The authors note that the delayed-memory asymmetry may instead reflect the confounded laboratory cluster.

grade.reasoning: Double-blind placebo-controlled studies, mostly within-person, start high; down one level for risk of bias (the pooled studies were not appraised, and the trial read in full is at some concerns) and one for publication bias (allowing for possibly missing studies shrinks three of the four estimates): low. Rated as worded: at most small average improvements on laboratory tests after a single dose in healthy adults; 'is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). The clearest effect is on inhibitory control, about a fifth of a standard deviation and unchanged by trim-and-fill; the working-memory and short-term memory effects lose significance after correction; the medium delayed-memory effect is reported but not adopted as an independent finding, because it rests mainly on one laboratory's successive low-dose studies in men, which are not independent replications (METHODS §6.3), and nearly halves after correction. Overlap: the trial is one of the review's included studies and supplied within-person correlations for its change-score metric, and both papers come from the same laboratory, so they are not independent of each other. Status replicated: the review's pooled studies come from many laboratories, and for inhibitory control 24 studies show no measurable heterogeneity. The trial's perceived-enhancement result is a single study's finding from one uncorrected test (p = .05) without a blinding check; it is reported as measured, not as proof of an illusion, and the authors' word 'reliable' is not adopted. The review's suggestion that a small effect could decide an examination was not studied and is not used. Funding: the trial by the US Office of Naval Research; the review names none; neither paper has a competing-interest statement. Doses appear only as study conditions.

statement: In children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) and adults with ADHD in double-blind randomized trials of prescribed medicines, analysed at the time closest to 12 weeks (in the blood-pressure review the trials lasted a median of 7 weeks), amphetamine medicines compared with methylphenidate were associated with a slightly larger reduction in clinician-rated ADHD symptoms, a difference the review itself rates as low certainty and that rests partly on indirect comparisons in children and adolescents and only on indirect comparisons in adults, while stopping a trial because of side effects and the rises in blood pressure and pulse did not differ significantly between the two, without being shown to be equal (Cortese et al., 2018; Farhat et al., 2025). The one blinded trial here that gave children both drugs found about the same number of side-effect complaints on each but rated them somewhat more severe on dexamphetamine, at one fixed dose of each and with no placebo (Efron et al., 1997). Benefit: in a network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind trials to April 2017 (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults and 1 in both; 14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults; symptom analyses in 10,068 and 8131), both medicines reduced clinician-rated core symptoms more than placebo, amphetamines by a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 1.02 in children and adolescents and 0.79 in adults and methylphenidate by 0.78 and 0.49 (all four of moderate certainty by the review's GRADE ratings); amphetamines against methylphenidate gave SMDs of −0.24 (95% CI −0.44 to −0.05) in children and adolescents and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05) in adults, both of low certainty, an advantage the authors call marginal in children and adolescents. Teachers' ratings were available for methylphenidate (SMD −0.82 against placebo, low certainty) but not for amphetamines, and clinicians' global improvement ratings did not differ significantly between the two (no estimate printed). The abstract calls the symptom differences head-to-head comparisons, but they are network estimates: by the authors' account head-to-head trials were few and comparisons between drugs were frequently based on indirect evidence, and the network plot shows no trial comparing the two in adults. Stopping because of side effects (11,018 children and adolescents and 5362 adults): against placebo, the odds of leaving a trial because of side effects were higher with amphetamines (odds ratio 2.30, 1.36 to 3.89, in children and adolescents; 3.26, 1.54 to 6.92, in adults; moderate certainty) and with methylphenidate in adults (2.39, 1.40 to 4.08, high certainty), but not clearly with methylphenidate in children and adolescents (1.44, 0.90 to 2.31, low certainty); amphetamines against methylphenidate gave 1.60 (0.94 to 2.73, low certainty) in children and adolescents and 1.36 (0.54 to 3.43, very low certainty) in adults, neither significant, so more stopping on amphetamines is neither shown nor ruled out. The article gives odds ratios only, not how many people stopped. The authors' preference for methylphenidate in children and adolescents and amphetamines in adults rests on each drug's comparison with placebo (in children and adolescents methylphenidate was the only medicine with better acceptability than placebo and, unlike amphetamines, was not worse tolerated than placebo), not on a difference between the two. Both lowered weight against placebo (SMDs −0.71 in children and adolescents and −0.60 in adults with amphetamines, −0.77 and −0.74 with methylphenidate; no comparison of the two is printed). Blood pressure and pulse: in a second network meta-analysis by an overlapping team that reused and extended the first one's searches to January 2024 (102 trials; 13,315 children and adolescents, mean age 11, and 9387 adults, mean age 35; median trial length 7 weeks; 87 of the 102 trials industry funded), the average rises against placebo, which the authors describe as small on average, were: in children and adolescents, systolic pressure +1.81 mm Hg, diastolic +2.42 and pulse +3.88 beats a minute with methylphenidate; +0.87 (not significant), +1.93 and +1.78 (not significant) with amphetamines; and +1.76, +2.29 and +4.17 with lisdexamfetamine, analysed separately; in adults, all of very low certainty, +1.66, +1.6 and +4.37 with methylphenidate, +2.3, +1.91 and +5.18 with amphetamines, and +1.62 (not significant), +3.07 and +5.07 with lisdexamfetamine. Neither amphetamines nor lisdexamfetamine differed significantly from methylphenidate in either age group: amphetamines minus methylphenidate, systolic −0.94 mm Hg (−2.33 to 0.44, high certainty) in children and adolescents and +0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults, diastolic −0.49 (−1.87 to 0.88) and +0.31 (−1.87 to 2.49) (editors' sign reversal of the printed methylphenidate-minus-amphetamines values), and pulse −2.1 beats a minute (−4.25 to 0.06) and +0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90). All adult trials were placebo-controlled, so every adult comparison between medicines is indirect; restricted to licensed doses, the authors report that only amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine were still consistently associated with higher blood pressure than placebo in adults (numbers only in the appendix, not read); only four trials gave 24-week results and none longer; and these are group averages, which the authors say some people may exceed. The head-to-head trial: 125 children aged 5 to 15 (114 boys) referred to a hospital clinic in Melbourne took dexamphetamine, an amphetamine, and methylphenidate in identical capsules twice a day for two weeks each, in random order, with investigators, families, children and teachers blind to the order. On parents' ratings of 17 listed complaints (0 absent, 1 to 9 for severity; a scale without published norms), the mean number of complaints was 7.64 on dexamphetamine and 7.19 on methylphenidate (not different) against 8.19 before treatment, and the mean severity of the complaints reported was 3.73 against 3.24 (significant; 4.08 before treatment); six items were rated more severe on dexamphetamine (trouble sleeping 3.61 against 2.69, irritability 3.65 against 2.94, proneness to crying 3.4 against 2.7, anxiousness 2.71 against 2.07, sadness or unhappiness 2.43 against 1.69, nightmares 0.79 against 0.48), none on methylphenidate, and two children stopped on each drug because of severe effects. Many complaints were already reported before any medicine (irritability in 102 of the 125 children, anxiousness in 96), and only poor appetite (43 before, 74 on dexamphetamine, 69 on methylphenidate) and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine (67 before, 88) were more frequent on a drug than before; with no placebo, changes from before treatment cannot be attributed to the drugs. Each drug was given at one fixed dose set by body weight, and the paper does not report whether the two doses worked equally well (parents rated 86 children improved on dexamphetamine and 90 on methylphenidate, not tested), so the difference in severity may reflect the doses chosen. These are prescribed medicines at licensed or guideline doses, studied over weeks in people diagnosed with ADHD; the papers say nothing about long-term use or about use without a prescription. Psychosis, which neither review studied, is a separate answer (see the answer on psychosis after starting amphetamine or methylphenidate). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Adderall or Ritalin: which works better, and which has more side effects? In reviews of short trials in people with ADHD, both amphetamine medicines (such as Adderall) and methylphenidate (such as Ritalin) eased symptoms clearly more than a dummy pill. On doctors' ratings amphetamine came out slightly ahead, but the review rated that difference low certainty: few trials compared the two directly, none in adults, so the comparison mostly runs through trials against a dummy pill. People did not clearly stop a trial because of side effects more often on one than on the other, though a difference could not be ruled out; compared with a dummy pill, more stopped on amphetamine at every age, and on methylphenidate in adults. Both lowered weight. Over about 7 weeks, blood pressure rose by about 1 to 3 points (mm Hg) and pulse by about 2 to 5 beats a minute on average compared with a dummy pill, with no clear difference between the two medicines. In the one blinded trial that gave 125 children both medicines, two weeks each and with no dummy pill, parents reported about as many complaints on each, but rated sleep and mood complaints (trouble sleeping, irritability, crying, anxiousness, sadness, nightmares) a little more severe on dexamphetamine, a kind of amphetamine; many of these complaints were already there before any medicine. The trials lasted weeks, not years, and they say nothing about taking these medicines without a prescription.

statement: In 13- to 25-year-olds with ADHD in two US commercial insurance claims databases who started a prescribed stimulant between 2004 and 2015, starting amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine) compared with starting methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate) was associated with a higher rate of a new psychotic episode treated with an antipsychotic, although such episodes were rare after either: among 221,846 people matched one to one on a propensity score (110,923 in each group), 343 had an episode over a median follow-up of 113 to 162 days by group and database (about 4 to 5 months), about 1 in 650 (343 of 221,846 is 1 in 647, editors' calculation; the paper says approximately 1 in 660); 106 episodes followed methylphenidate and 237 amphetamine, 1.78 against 2.83 episodes per 1,000 person-years of use, a hazard ratio of 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09), prespecified as the primary analysis, and a difference of about 1 episode per 1,000 person-years (1.05, editors' calculation) (Moran et al., 2019). The paper's closing sentence, that the risk was about twice as high with amphetamine, rests on the crude shares of patients (0.21% against 0.10%), which do not allow for the longer time people who started amphetamine stayed in the study (median 155 against 113 days in one database and 162 against 123 in the other; from the printed counts and rates, about 83,700 against 59,600 person-years, editors' calculation): the two rates give a ratio of 1.59 (editors' calculation), and the hazard ratio is 1.65. The comparison is not randomized. People were matched on what the claims record (age, year, sex, region, insurance, markers of ADHD severity, other psychiatric diagnoses and medicines, recorded substance use disorders, type of prescriber and use of care; largest standardized difference 0.02); in the full unmatched cohort of 337,919 the hazard ratio was 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77) unadjusted and 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92) adjusted; two stricter definitions of psychosis gave 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) and 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22); emergency or inpatient care for alcohol, cannabis, opioid or other substance use disorders and for depression without psychosis, used as checks, did not differ between the groups (hazard ratios 0.91 to 1.12, all intervals including 1); and, by the authors' bias analysis, cannabis use would have had to be 97.0% among amphetamine starters, against an estimated 35.8% among people with ADHD, to explain the finding (assuming that any cannabis use doubles the risk of psychosis). Claims cannot show unrecorded drug use, early symptoms before psychosis, family history, the dose, or whether the medicines were taken; amphetamine was prescribed more to older patients and by family or internal medicine doctors (72.5% of their patients, against 51.6% of paediatricians'); and people who switched to the other stimulant (13.8% of methylphenidate starters, 5.6% of amphetamine starters) stopped being followed at the switch. Episodes in the first 7 days were not counted, and the median time to an episode was 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Psychosis counted only when coded and treated with an antipsychotic within 60 days (positive predictive value 91.3% in a review of records by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug, 93.1% in an outside validation), so milder or untreated symptoms are not counted. Results by age, by type of prescriber and by formulation were post hoc, with no test of whether subgroups differ. The people studied had commercial insurance; the authors say the results do not apply to people with public or no insurance, and the study says nothing about adults over 25, children under 13, use over years or use without a prescription. No other study on file measured psychosis with these medicines; the two network meta-analyses of trials did not study it. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Is psychosis more likely on amphetamine (as in Adderall) than on methylphenidate (as in Ritalin)? In one large US study of insurance records, a new psychotic episode treated with antipsychotic medicine was rare after starting either medicine, but somewhat more common after amphetamine. Among about 222,000 young people aged 13 to 25 with ADHD, matched on what their records showed, 343 had such an episode while followed for about 4 to 5 months, about 1 in 650. For every 1,000 people taking the medicine for a year, that was about 1.8 on methylphenidate and 2.8 on amphetamine: about 1.65 times the rate, or about 1 extra episode per 1,000 people a year. The authors' own summary, about twice as high, does not allow for amphetamine starters being followed for longer. The finding held with stricter definitions of psychosis, and emergency or hospital care for alcohol or cannabis use disorders was not more common after amphetamine. But it is not a trial: the records cannot show drug use that was never recorded, early signs of illness, the dose, or whether the pills were taken, and the study says nothing about longer use, adults over 25, or use without a prescription.
